channel.title: Daily Recap — 🔬 AI Research
channel.description: What happened in 🔬 AI Research, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: Leaked draft of Anthropic's AI regulatory bill draws sharp criticism
item.description:
A purported draft of an AI regulatory bill that Anthropic is reportedly shopping to lawmakers has leaked, and Zvi Moshowitz's early read is harsh: he calls the draft unacceptable and troubling, arguing that even with its apparent bugs fixed, it would be a bad piece of legislation.

Why it matters: Anthropic has been positioning itself as the most policy-engaged of the frontier labs, and a leaked draft from them — rather than from regulators — is a sign that labs are actively trying to shape the rules they will be governed by. For researchers and practitioners, the substance of the bill matters less right now than the signal: the industry is entering a phase where companies write the first drafts of their own regulation, and early drafts deserve close scrutiny before they gain momentum.

Sources

  • The Zvi: Leaked Anthropic Draft AI Regulatory Bill Is Unacceptable and Troubling

item.title: AI code review is being rewired: "did a human read the code?" is the wrong question
item.description:
Simon Willison spotlighted a rethink of code review for the AI era, quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang: "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for the real question — what could go wrong with this change, and which check, automated or human, is the right one to catch it? The sharper framing is changing when review happens: instead of a gate at the end of the road (write the code, open a PR, wait for a colleague), review now runs continuously, "more like spellcheck while you write."

Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look, catching routine mistakes early and saving team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. It's a compact statement of how seriously the review workflow is being rewired: the bottleneck is no longer reviewer availability but deciding which checks genuinely need a human eye.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang

item.title: AINews: agents are disproving polysemanticity and boosting interpretability
item.description:
Nick Cammarata is making major claims in a new Latent.Space AINews episode: AI agents are helping disprove polysemanticity — the long-standing finding that individual neurons respond to many unrelated concepts — and in doing so are greatly improving interpretability and alignment research.

If the claim holds up, it's significant: polysemanticity has been one of the core obstacles to reading neural networks' internals, and resolving it would give safety researchers a much clearer window into model behavior. That said, the feed entry gives only the episode's headline, so treat this as a pointer rather than a verdict — the episode itself is where to judge whether the evidence matches the ambition. Worth a listen for anyone tracking whether interpretability is on the verge of a step change.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Agents disprove Polysemanticity; greatly improve Interpretability & Alignment

item.title: Modal hits $1B ARR and a $16B Series D — NYC's newest AI infra decacorn
item.description:
Modal, the serverless AI infrastructure company, has reached $1 billion in annualized recurring revenue and closed a $16 billion Series D — tripling both usage and valuation in five months, and growing roughly 15x in a year. That makes it New York's newest AI infrastructure decacorn.

The numbers underline where the real money in AI is concentrating: not just in models, but in the sandboxed compute platforms that run them. Modal's bet is that "sandboxes are all you need" — ephemeral, isolated compute for AI workloads — and the market is now valuing that proposition at decacorn levels.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Modal's $1B ARR, $16B Series D makes it NYC's newest AI Infra Decacorn, 3x usage and 3x valuation in 5 months, 15x in 1 yr

item.title: Nvidia scales Indic pretraining to 2.8 trillion tokens with an open data pipeline
item.description:
Nvidia published a technical post on scaling Indic-language pretraining to 2.8 trillion tokens, along with an open data generation pipeline for building large multilingual corpora. Indic languages have historically been underserved in pretraining data, and this is one of the largest efforts to close that gap.

The open pipeline matters as much as the token count: reproducible data generation lets other teams build high-quality pretraining sets for underrepresented languages. For a research community increasingly focused on multilingual evaluation, this is genuinely useful infrastructure.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline

item.title: IBM's Granite Switch 4.1: chat, decisions, and speech from one endpoint
item.description:
IBM released Granite Switch 4.1, which unifies chat, decision-making, and speech capabilities behind a single endpoint. Rather than orchestrating separate models for conversation, reasoning, and voice, teams can route all three through one interface.

It's a pragmatic enterprise play: fewer endpoints to manage, one model family to evaluate, and less plumbing in production. The "switch" framing suggests the model dynamically handles the different modes, which — if it holds up in practice — simplifies a lot of real-world agent deployments.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint

item.title: Chirp Pong: a two-player phone game networked through sound
item.description:
Simon Willison built Chirp Pong, a two-player competitive Pong-like game played on two separate phones, where game state is transmitted between devices as audio chirps picked up by the Web microphone API — no network, no pairing, just sound. He built it with Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code, adding graphical and gameplay twists beyond plain Pong.

It's a delightful proof of concept: acoustic networking as a fallback channel for local multiplayer, running in static HTML on ordinary phones. The experiment shows how fast an idea can go from "is this even feasible?" to working demo with modern coding agents — which is arguably the real story.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Chirp Pong

item.title: Anthropic's investor day: $16.8B Q3, 11% margins, and a distillation edge
item.description:
Anthropic briefed investors ahead of its IPO, and the FT's reporting — summarized by Simon Willison — fills in the trajectory: roughly $4.8B in Q1, $11.5B in Q2, $16.8B in Q3, with adjusted operating margins of 11% excluding stock-based comp. Strikingly, Q3 brought in $1.70 of revenue for every $1 spent on compute.

That ratio is the number to watch: it suggests Anthropic's distillation and efficiency work is converting compute spend into revenue at a healthy multiple, not just burning capital for growth. As the IPO approaches, these are the economics the market will price — and they'll set the benchmark for every frontier lab's fundraising story.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO

item.title: Gemini 4 Argon goes GA; Vals AI and CursorBench confirm the claims
item.description:
Google’s Gemini 4 Argon went generally available on October 14, arriving at the AI Engineer NYC conference where independent benchmarks were the main validation story. Vals AI released its benchmark results and CursorBench figures largely confirmed Google’s published claims – the AINews newsletter had already made Argon the title story two weeks earlier based on Google’s numbers, and the independents mostly agreed.

The milestone matters less as a capability leap than as a credibility marker: when multiple independent eval suites converge with vendor claims, it suggests the frontier’s public benchmarks are staying honest, and Argon’s GA status puts a verified top-tier model into developers’ hands right as agentic coding tooling heats up.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] AI Engineer NYC: Gemini 4 Argon, Vals AI Benchmarks

item.title: HiRO-ACEv2: 3 km extreme-weather simulation at a fraction of the cost
item.description:
The Allen Institute for AI’s new HiRO-ACEv2 model simulates extreme weather at 3 km resolution – the kind of fine-grained modeling that used to demand massive supercomputer budgets – at a fraction of the historical cost. The write-up on the Hugging Face Blog lays out how the emulator reaches high-resolution forecasts without the usual compute bill.

This is AI-as-science-infrastructure in its most compelling form: cheaper high-resolution weather models mean more frequent extreme-weather simulations, better local forecasts, and more researchers able to run them. If the cost reductions hold at scale, this class of emulator could quietly upgrade climate and disaster modeling for everyone.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost

item.title: Leash Bio’s lab-in-the-loop: taming DEL assays for AI agents that think like chemists
item.description:
Leash Bio’s Ian Quigley described how the company tamed DNA-encoded library (DEL) screening – the notoriously finicky assay that “traumatizes everyone” – and used the resulting data to catch models that were cheating on their evaluations. That same high-quality assay data turns out to be exactly what AI agents need to start learning to think like chemists.

It’s a clean example of the lab-in-the-loop flywheel that drug discovery is converging on: better wet-lab data exposes model shortcuts, which forces more honest training, which yields agents that can actually reason about chemistry rather than pattern-match their way to fake results. The interesting research frontier here is data quality, not just model size.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: Lab-in-the-Loop at Compute Speed — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio

item.title: Crossing the threshold: how labs are structuring autonomy and safety in financial agents
item.description:
At AI Engineer New York, engineers from frontier labs and financial firms dug into one of the sharpest deployment questions in AI: how do you give financial agents enough autonomy to be useful while keeping consequential decisions under human control? The discussion covered how OpenAI and Anthropic are each approaching the autonomy-safety tradeoff for agents that move money and execute trades.

Finance is the proving ground for consequential-agent design because the failure modes are measured in dollars and the compliance bar is already high. Whatever governance patterns emerge here – bounded autonomy tiers, approval gates, audit-first architectures – are likely to become the template for agent deployment in every other regulated industry.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: Crossing the Threshold: How OpenAI and Anthropic Approach Autonomy and Safety in Financial Agents

item.title: Zvi: the safety culture at the frontier labs is broken
item.description:
Zvi Mowshowitz argues that the frontier labs lack the deep, robust safety culture they need – that safety practices at the leading labs are performative or thin rather than embedded in how work actually gets done. His call: the labs need genuine safety culture, not just safety teams.

The piece lands in a week full of corroborating signals – self-improvement timelines being walked back, alignment work lagging capabilities, insider threats at OpenAI itself – and it cuts to the core complaint: the race dynamics reward shipping over caution, and no amount of eval benchmarks substitutes for an organization that takes safety as seriously as it takes training runs.

Sources

  • The Zvi: The Safety Culture at the Labs is Broken

item.title: AI is mass decompiling games – a boom for preservation, a threat to the industry
item.description:
Indie developer Popcar’s post on the wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games – enabling weird mashups between games and a boom in preservation projects that get old games running on new hardware, often in the browser via WebAssembly – gets the Simon Willison treatment, capturing both the delight and the dread.

The duality is the story: the same capability that rescues gaming history and democratizes remixing also means “the entire tech industry is about to explode,” since anybody can decompile anything. It’s one of the clearest real-world demonstrations yet that AI has dissolved the practical barrier around reverse engineering – with huge consequences for preservation, piracy, and the economics of proprietary software.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.

item.title: Anthropic ditched Git after AI coding agents pushed merges past 30,000 a day
item.description:
Anthropic rebuilt its source control from scratch after AI coding agents blew past Git's limits. In May 2026 the company merged about 2,500 code changes per day; by September it was merging over 30,000 per day. That twelvefold jump forced Anthropic to build its own custom alternative to Git.

Simon Willison annotated Anthropic's chart with the public release dates of its 2026 models, making the cause legible: each coding-agent release ratcheted the curve upward. It's one of the clearest real-world measurements yet of agentic coding at scale — and a sign that developer tooling built for humans is being rewritten for machine-speed commit rates.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Redesigning source control at Anthropic

item.title: Meta's MSL emerges as a frontier lab with Muse Wonder, rated at Claude 5.5 tier
item.description:
Meta's MSL unit released Muse Wonder and Wonder Full, models positioned at Anthropic's Claude 5.5 tier — and independent benchmarks already show Muse Wonder Full trading blows with Claude Opus 5.5 and leading Google's new Gemini 4 Argon.

Latent.Space's AINews called it "MSL's emergence as a frontier lab is finally complete," and the timing matters: Meta has gone from fast follower to a genuine three-way race with Anthropic and Google at the top of the capability ladder. The frontier is no longer a two-lab story.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Meta Muse Wonder & Wonder Full: MSL’s Claude 5.5-tier Frontier Model

item.title: LiquidAI releases LFM2.5-24B-A2B for fast, private on-device agents
item.description:
LiquidAI released LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24-billion-parameter model designed to run fast, private agentic workloads on-device, announced via the Hugging Face Blog.

The pitch fits the day's bigger current: Anthropic's own research warns small models are getting capable enough to self-replicate across consumer hardware, so building capable models that run locally and privately is increasingly the differentiator. For developers, a 24B model that handles agent workloads on-device narrows the gap between cloud-scale agents and ones that never leave the machine.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

item.title: Dyna-2 bets on world action models for hour-long robot autonomy
item.description:
Latent.Space's first robotics podcast dug into Dyna Robotics' Dyna-2, a push toward general-purpose physical agents with hour-long autonomy. The core bet: "world action models" — models that don't just perceive or plan, but predict and execute physical action — as the next frontier of physical AI.

Hour-long autonomy matters because most demos still collapse within minutes; sustained, reliable physical task execution is the gap between lab robotics and useful machines. The interview with Dyna's chief scientist frames physical AI as the field's next scaling frontier after language and reasoning.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: Dyna-2: General Purpose Physical Agents with Hour-Long Autonomy — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
